setup.t: Set up Cowork for the Academy
setup.lead: You'll arrange your screen, add the Academy's starter folder to your computer, open Cowork on it, and check that Cowork can work with the files inside.
setup.why: Every mission uses this one folder and its practice files, so nothing needs downloading later and your work stays in one place.
setup.result: Cowork open on your Cowork Academy folder, ready for every mission.

steps.goal: Get into the Claude desktop app, because Cowork only runs there and not in a browser tab.
steps.title: Open the Claude desktop app
steps.do: Open the Claude app on your computer and sign in with your work account. Cowork runs in the desktop app, not in a browser tab.
steps.see: The Claude app is open and signed in.
steps.stuck: No desktop app yet? Use the button above to download it. If you can't find Cowork once it's open, your plan may not include it yet. Ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Set up your screen so you can read each step here and do it in Claude without switching back and forth.
steps.title: Put the windows side by side
steps.do: Arrange this page and the Claude app side by side, so you can read a step here and do it there.
steps.see: The Academy on one half of your screen and Claude on the other.
steps.stuck: On a small laptop screen, keep both open and switch between them with Cmd+Tab on a Mac or Alt+Tab on Windows.

steps.goal: Put the Academy's practice files on your computer in one folder, so every later mission already has what it needs.
steps.title: Get the starter folder
steps.do: Download the starter folder below. Open the downloaded zip file, then move the Cowork Academy folder inside it into your Documents folder.
steps.see: A folder called Cowork Academy in Documents, with practice files inside such as orders.csv, customer-feedback.csv, support-tickets.csv, customer-messages.txt and team-notes.txt.
steps.stuck: On a Mac, double-click the zip in Downloads, then drag the Cowork Academy folder to Documents. On Windows, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then move the Cowork Academy folder to Documents.

steps.goal: Point Cowork at the Cowork Academy folder, because it can only see and change files in the folder you give it.
steps.title: Start a Cowork task on the folder
steps.do: In the Claude app, switch to Cowork and start a new task. When it asks which folder it can work in, choose Cowork Academy in Documents.
steps.see: An empty Cowork task with a message box, working in your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.stuck: If it didn't ask for a folder, look for an option to choose or change the working folder near the message box. Still stuck? Check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Confirm Cowork can read your folder and create a file in it, so you know setup worked before the first mission.
steps.title: Check Cowork can see the files
steps.do: Paste this into the message box and press Enter.
steps.prompt: List the files in this folder and tell me in one sentence what each one seems to contain. Then create a file called hello.txt that says: My Cowork Academy folder.
steps.see: A list of the practice files with a short description of each, and a new hello.txt in your Cowork Academy folder. Notice that it described files you know are there, which shows it's in the right folder.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks your permission before creating the file, allow it. If it says it can't see any files, the task is pointed at the wrong folder: start a new task and choose Cowork Academy.

steps.q: You’re in a new mission and Cowork says it can’t find orders.csv. What’s the most likely cause?
options: The task is working in a different folder
The file needs to be emailed to Cowork first
Cowork only reads files you paste into the task
steps.why: Cowork works with the folder you chose for the task. Start a new task on Cowork Academy and the file will be there. Emailing or pasting files isn’t needed.

safety.t: Use Claude the right way at work
safety.lead: A six-question quiz on what's fine to share with Claude, what needs approval first, and what never belongs in an AI tool. Then you'll practice spotting private details.
safety.why: People who know where the lines are use AI confidently instead of nervously. Your company's own AI policy always takes priority over general guidance.
safety.result: Your quiz score, plus practice spotting private details before they reach any AI tool.

think.scene: At work: three habits cover most of the risk. Keep private things private, let Claude draft while you decide and send, and check numbers before you share them.
think.ask: Which information in your job should never leave your company's approved tools?

steps.title: Take the quiz
steps.intro: For each situation, choose what you'd do. You'll see the answer straight away.

items.s: Pasting a product description from your company’s public website so Claude can rewrite it more clearly.
items.why: It's already public, so there's nothing private to protect.

items.s: Giving Claude your system login and password so it can pull a report for you.
items.why: Never share passwords with any AI tool. Sign in yourself and give Claude the exported file.

items.s: Uploading a customer list with names, email addresses and phone numbers to find duplicate entries.
items.why: Customer personal details need your company’s approval. Often the better move is to remove those columns first.

items.s: Letting Claude send a reply to an upset customer without you reading it first.
items.why: Claude drafts, you read and send. You know the customer and the policy, and you’re responsible for what goes out.

items.s: Uploading a signed supplier contract to get a plain-English summary of the renewal and termination terms.
items.why: Contracts are usually confidential. Check your company's AI policy or ask your manager before uploading one.

items.s: Pasting last month’s team totals (no names) to make a chart for an internal meeting.
items.why: Internal numbers without personal data are usually fine in your company's approved Claude. Check the chart before you share it.

steps.goal: Try finding the private details on your own first, so you can compare your eye with Cowork's and learn what to look for.
steps.title: Spot the private details yourself
steps.do: Read this made-up message and count every private or sensitive detail before going on: "Hi team, Maria Gomez (555-201-3344, company card ending 4417) is on medical leave after surgery. Her building door code was 8812. Please reimburse her travel costs."
steps.see: Your own count. There are four kinds of private detail in it.
steps.stuck: Look for anything that identifies a person, could be used to get in somewhere, relates to payment, or reveals health information.

steps.goal: See what Cowork flags and how it rewrites the message safely, so you learn what to remove before sharing anything.
steps.title: Compare with Cowork
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter. Everything in it is made up, which is the only reason it's okay to paste.
steps.prompt: List every private or sensitive detail in this message, then rewrite it so it’s safe to share with the wider team: "Hi team, Maria Gomez (555-201-3344, company card ending 4417) is on medical leave after surgery. Her building door code was 8812. Please reimburse her travel costs."
steps.see: Cowork lists the employee’s name and phone number, the card digits, the medical leave and the door code, and gives a rewritten message without them. Did you find all four kinds?
steps.stuck: If Cowork's list differs from yours, ask it: "Is there anything else a careful person would remove?"

steps.q: An HR coordinator wants to paste an employee’s email, including the employee’s home address, into Claude to draft a reply. What’s the best advice?
options: Paste it all, since Claude is approved
Leave out the address, then draft
Don’t use Claude for HR messages at all
steps.why: The reply doesn’t need the home address, so leave it out. Claude is still useful for drafting; it’s the unneeded personal detail that’s the risk.

ideas.lead: Cowork interviews you about your week, using what you noted during the Academy, and suggests where it could save you time. Then you'll write up your best idea for Spark.
ideas.why: This is the point of the Academy: the best improvements come from the people who do the work.
ideas.result: One clear idea, written up and ready to submit in Spark.

think.scene: At work: a payroll clerk, a store manager and a claims adjuster each save two hours a week. That is 100 hours a year each, and across a team it becomes a project leadership will fund.
think.ask: Your best idea, in one sentence

steps.goal: Let Cowork ask about your week, so repetitive work you've stopped noticing comes to the surface.
steps.title: Get interviewed about your week
steps.do: Copy this prompt (it already includes your role and the notes you saved during the Academy), paste it into your Cowork task and press Enter. Answer each question in a sentence or two.
steps.prompt: I work in {{ROLE}}. {{NOTES}}Interview me about my job. Ask me 5 short questions, one at a time, about what I do each week, which tasks are repetitive or manual, which reports I build, and where I wait on information from other people. Wait for my answer before asking the next question.
steps.see: Cowork asks its first question and waits for your answer.
steps.stuck: If it asks all 5 questions at once, answer them all in one message. That works too.

steps.goal: Turn your answers into five concrete ideas with time savings, so you can choose which one is worth pursuing.
steps.title: Rank your top five opportunities
steps.do: After your last answer, paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Based on my answers, list my top 5 opportunities to use Claude. For each, say what Cowork would do (a skill, a connector, a report, a dashboard or a scheduled task), roughly how many hours a month it could save, and whether I could build it myself or would need help.
steps.see: A numbered list of 5 opportunities, each with what Cowork would do and an estimate of hours saved. Notice which ones save the most hours.
steps.stuck: If the ideas feel generic, add: "Make them specific to what I told you about my week."

steps.goal: Test the first step of your favorite idea, so your Spark write-up comes from something you've seen work.
steps.title: Optional: try the best one
steps.do: If you have 10 minutes, pick the opportunity that would help you most and try its first step. Otherwise, skip to the next step.
steps.prompt: Let's try the first step of opportunity number [the number you picked, e.g. 2] right now, using files in this folder or realistic made-up data.
steps.see: Cowork starts on your idea, for example drafting the first version of a report, a template or a checklist.
steps.stuck: If it needs data you don't have, ask it to use the practice files in this folder instead.

steps.q: Your manager will pick two ideas from the team to fund this quarter. Which submission gives them the most to go on?
options: A dashboard for everything so leadership can see all of our numbers
Use AI more across the finance team to save time each week
Monday report: 2 hrs a week, Cowork builds it from the export
steps.why: It names the task, how often it happens, the time it takes and what Cowork would do, so it can be judged and built. The others sound bigger but give nothing to act on.
